extracted.intended_audience: writers, storytellers, students of narratology and comparative mythology
extracted.subtask_description: Use Joseph Campbell's monomyth (the Hero's Journey) as a structural template for plotting or analysing stories: a sequence of stages (often grouped as Departure, Initiation, Return) through which a protagonist passes and is transformed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departure / Separation (three-act grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of three major sections in Campbell's organization of the 17 stages: Departure (also Separation) — the hero leaves the ordinary world and begins the adventure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an act-level structural beat for plotting; contains specific sub-stages (Ordinary World, Call to Adventure, Refusal of the Call, Meeting with the Mentor/Supernatural Aid, Crossing the First Threshold, Belly of the Whale).

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiation (three-act grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Second major section in the monomyth containing the trials and transformations the hero undergoes in the special world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often subdivided (Descent and Initiation) and includes stages such as Road of Trials, Meeting with the Goddess, Woman as Temptress, Atonement with the Father, Apotheosis, and The Ultimate Boon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return (three-act grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Final major section: the hero returns to the ordinary world transformed and brings back a boon or wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contains stages like Refusal of the Return, The Magic Flight, Rescue from Without, Crossing of the Return Threshold, Master of the Two Worlds, and Freedom to Live; focuses on reintegration and sharing the boon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary World
rubrics_metrics.description: The hero begins in a situation of normality from which some information is received that acts as a call to head off into the unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish the protagonist's baseline life, context, and what is at stake so the later change is evident; examples cited include Theseus arriving in Athens and Odysseus being driven by Poseidon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call to Adventure
rubrics_metrics.description: Information or an event that prompts the hero to leave the ordinary world and undertake an adventure into the unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The call can come voluntarily, be thrust upon the hero, or even arise from a casual or accidental incident; use vivid, specific triggers to move the plot from ordinary to extraordinary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal of the Call
rubrics_metrics.description: When first presented with the call, the future hero often refuses due to duty, fear, insecurity, or sense of inadequacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use refusal to dramatize internal conflict and stakes; Campbell notes refusal can convert the adventure into a negative state and deepen the need for transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supernatural Aid / Meeting with the Mentor
rubrics_metrics.description: Once committed to the quest, a guide or magical helper appears to assist the hero, often providing talismans or advice that will aid later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentors can be literal or symbolic; the aid reassures that unconscious or larger forces support the hero's path — useful for providing tools, knowledge, or symbolic gifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crossing the First Threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: The hero actually enters the field of adventure, leaving known limits behind and encountering the threshold guardian(s) and unknown rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict a clear point-of-no-return with guardians/barriers and rising danger; this transition establishes the 'special world' and the rules that govern it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belly of the Whale
rubrics_metrics.description: Represents the final separation from the hero's known world and self — a transit into rebirth; the hero is swallowed into the unknown and appears to die before being reborn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbolize deep inward change or apparent death/rebirth (text cites Jonah's three days in the fish and Star Wars trash-compactor scene); use this beat to mark irreversible transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Road of Trials
rubrics_metrics.description: A series of tests and ordeals the hero must undergo to begin transformation; often includes failures and frequently occurs in threes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure sequences of escalating tests, include setbacks, and show covert aid from earlier mentors; classic motifs include slaying dragons and overcoming barriers, producing preliminary victories and glimpses of the wondrous.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Meeting with the Goddess
rubrics_metrics.description: The point where the hero encounters a figure (often female) who represents unconditional love, receives gifts or aid, or experiences a unifying vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be literal or symbolic; represents attainment of a significant boon (sometimes expressed as a mystical marriage) and tests the hero's capacity to receive life-affirming power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Woman as the Temptress
rubrics_metrics.description: The hero faces temptations (often sensual or material) that may lead them to abandon or stray from the quest; 'woman' here is a metaphor for earthly temptation, not necessarily a literal woman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this beat to reveal the hero's weaknesses and priorities; resist shallow moralizing by making temptations thematically relevant to the hero's arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atonement with the Father (Abyss)
rubrics_metrics.description: The hero must confront and be initiated by whatever holds ultimate power in their life; often symbolized by the father-figure or a supreme authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central ordeal and turning point; dramatize the ego-annihilating confrontation that prepares the hero for apotheosis and the ultimate boon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apotheosis
rubrics_metrics.description: A point of realization in which a greater understanding is achieved; the hero gains a higher perspective and is resolved for the next phase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a clear epiphany or shift in perception to signal inner transformation; this readies the hero for reclaiming or obtaining the boon.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Ultimate Boon
rubrics_metrics.description: The achievement of the goal of the quest — the object of the search, often transcendent (elixir of life, holy grail, immortality, or spiritual illumination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the boon consequential and connected to earlier trials; Campbell notes guardians release such boons only to the duly proven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal of the Return
rubrics_metrics.description: After attaining bliss or enlightenment, the hero may not want to return to the ordinary world to bestow the boon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This beat highlights the tension between transcendent insight and mundane responsibility — use it to complicate the hero's reintegration.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Magic Flight
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the hero must escape with the boon, and the return journey can be as adventurous and dangerous as the outward quest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include pursuit, magical obstruction, and evasion as obstacles to delivering the boon; this can add tension and set up final stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rescue from Without
rubrics_metrics.description: The hero may need external help to be brought back to everyday life, especially if weakened by the adventure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This stage allows allies or society to play an active role in reintegrating the hero; shows that return may require communal effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crossing of the Return Threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: The returning hero must survive the impact of the ordinary world and retain the wisdom gained on the quest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray difficulties of translation between inner vision and everyday reality; the narrative should show how the hero integrates insights without losing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master of the Two Worlds
rubrics_metrics.description: The hero achieves a balance between material and spiritual (inner and outer) worlds and can pass between them with competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This beat signals maturity and the capacity to act effectively in both realms; useful as a penultimate felicity before final resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom to Live
rubrics_metrics.description: Having overcome fear (often fear of death), the hero attains freedom to live in the moment without anxieties about past or future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often the final state of the monomyth: depict a relaxed, life-affirming stance where the hero acts without clinging — a satisfying emotional resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Campbell's 17-stage inventory and variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Campbell lists seventeen stages of the monomyth but warns that not all myths contain all 17 stages explicitly; some focus on only one stage, and stages may appear in different order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the 17 stages as a flexible toolkit rather than prescriptive checklist; writers should select, reorder, or compress stages to fit their story's needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vogler / Practical adaptations for writers
rubrics_metrics.description: Christopher Vogler created a condensed practical guide (A Practical Guide to The Hero with a Thousand Faces / The Writer's Journey) adapting Campbell's ideas into a writer-friendly template.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Vogler's simplified beats as a compact blueprint for films and commercial storytelling; be aware adaptations often streamline or rename Campbell's stages for dramatic clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticisms and limitations of the monomyth (methodological & cultural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars and folklorists criticize Campbell for source-selection bias, vagueness, ethnocentrism, analytic overgeneralization, and a masculine focus; alternatives (Heroine's Journey, Virgin's Promise) have been proposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious applying the monomyth uncritically: respect cultural specificity, avoid erasing local variants, and consider gendered or cultural perspectives that demand different structural patterns.
